fixes.why: The agreed block says every reading takes the text to say believers are told to remain in the faith to the end, and cites Matthew 24:13. The third reading's own 'answers' takes Matthew 24:13 (and Colossians 1:23) to name what marks a genuine faith or to address groups, not to state a condition. So the verse cited as common ground is one the third reading reads differently, and the sentence is not clearly common to every reading.
fixes.fix: Replace the Matthew 24:13 passage with Acts 14:22, 'strengthening the souls of the disciples and encouraging them to continue in the faith.', and word the clause 'that believers are urged to continue in the faith'. Keep 'to the end' out of the agreed sentence.

fixes.why: 'and take them to mean what they say' implies the other readings do not take the warnings at face value. Reading 2's summary says its holders hold the warnings to be real, so the phrase is a verdict by contrast.
fixes.fix: Delete 'and take them to mean what they say:'. Read: '...addressed to people who have received salvation, and take them to mean that a person who has been saved can turn away and be lost, and that the one who remains in Christ is kept.'

fixes.why: 'Written in the first person plural, to the author's own readers' is stated as fact, but the reading that takes 'we' as rhetorical (reading 2) disputes what follows from it. Other notes in the card use 'Read as' for this reason.
fixes.fix: 'Read as addressed to the author's own readers, who are included in the "we".'

fixes.where: reading 1 passages: Galatians 5:4, Romans 11:22 and Colossians 1:23 notes
fixes.why: These notes state the reading's conclusion as the verse's content ('Believers addressed as having fallen away from grace'; 'Reconciliation stated with continuing in the faith as its condition'). Readings 2 and 3 answer exactly these points, so the notes pre-empt them.
fixes.fix: Galatians 5:4: 'Read as addressing believers who have fallen away from grace.' Romans 11:22: 'Read as a warning to the Gentile believers that they too will be cut off if they do not continue.' Colossians 1:23: 'Read as stating reconciliation with continuing in the faith as its condition.'

fixes.why: Hebrews 6:6 begins mid-sentence ('and then have fallen away'), so a reader of the card does not see who is described. The note points to 6:4-5 but the words that carry the argument (shared in the Holy Spirit, tasted the heavenly gift) are not shown. Reading 2's answer turns on exactly what those phrases describe, so the reader needs them to follow either side.
fixes.fix: Keep the 6:6 quote and add to its note the Berean text of 6:4: 'It is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, who have shared in the Holy Spirit,' (quoted from Hebrews 6:4).

fixes.why: The summary says the warnings are the means by which God keeps his people, but none of the eight cited passages says anything of the kind. Holders cite Hebrews 6:9 and Philippians 2:12-13 for this. The claim reads as unsupported on the card.
fixes.fix: Swap Romans 8:39 for Philippians 2:12-13 with quote 'For it is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose.' (Philippians 2:13), note 'Read with 2:12 as working out salvation while God works in the believer.' Keep Romans 8:30 as the Romans 8 passage. Alternatively add Hebrews 6:9: 'we are convinced of better things in your case-things that accompany salvation.'

fixes.why: 'and not by the believer's grip' sets the reading against an unnamed rival picture in which the believer holds on, a picture the other readings would not own (Catholic and Orthodox readers speak of grace, not grip). It is a contrast that casts the other readings.
fixes.fix: '...held by what Christ has done and by God's faithfulness.' Drop 'and not by the believer's grip'.

fixes.why: Eternal-security holders cite John 10:28-29 and Ephesians 1:13-14 among their first verses, and the card gives John 10:28 only to reading 2 and Ephesians 4:30 alone for the sealing. The sealing is more naturally shown with 1:13-14, where the Spirit is named 'the pledge of our inheritance'. A verse may sit in two readings (as 1 John 2:19 is answered across them), so this does not unbalance the count.
fixes.fix: Replace Ephesians 4:30 with Ephesians 1:13-14 (quote 'who is the pledge of our inheritance until the redemption of those who are God's possession, to the praise of His glory.', Ephesians 1:14), keeping Ephesians 4:30 in the note, or add John 10:28 here as well and say in its note that reading 2 holders cite it too.

fixes.why: 'The sealing is named as lasting until the day of redemption' reads 'for the day of redemption' as 'until'. The Berean has 'for', and readings 1 and 2 would read the phrase differently.
fixes.fix: 'Read as naming the sealing as lasting until the day of redemption.'

fixes.why: The card presents the question only as a debate among later traditions over how to harmonise the verses. A scholar of religion would expect it to say that the passages come from different authors and settings (Paul's letters, Hebrews, John, Peter) and that readers differ on whether those authors share one view. This is a setting, not a verdict, and is stated by holders of readings 2 and 3 in their answers.
fixes.fix: Add to the intro: 'The passages come from several New Testament writers, and readers differ on whether they hold one view or speak to different situations.'

summary: All 28 quotes are exact Berean words, the readings are stated in their holders' terms and the counts are balanced, but a few phrases ('mean what they say', 'the believer's grip') and several assertive notes lean, and the agreed block cites Matthew 24:13, which the third reading reads differently. Adding Hebrews 6:4-5, a verse that supports the 'warnings as means' claim in reading 2, and a neutral note about the passages' different authors would make the card fairer and easier to follow.
